blocks.text: Disappointed, K. took the letter and put it in his pocket. Even in the most favourable case the advantage that the recommendation could bring him was relatively smaller than the harm that lay in the manufacturer's knowing about his trial and in the painter's spreading the news further. He could hardly force himself to thank the manufacturer, who was already on his way to the door, with a few words. "I'll go there," he said, as he took his leave of the manufacturer at the door, "or, since I'm very busy just now, write to him and ask him to come to my office some time." "I knew," said the manufacturer, "that you would find the best way out. Though I did think you would rather avoid inviting people like this Titorelli into the bank in order to talk with him here about the trial. Nor is it always advantageous to let letters out of one's hands to such people. But you have surely thought everything through and know what you may do." K. nodded and accompanied the manufacturer on through the anteroom. But despite his outward calm he was greatly alarmed at himself. He had really only said that he would write to Titorelli in order somehow to show the manufacturer that he valued the recommendation and was at once considering the possibilities of meeting with Titorelli, but if he had regarded Titorelli's assistance as valuable, he would not have hesitated actually to write to him either. The dangers, however, that this might bring in its train he had recognized only through the manufacturer's remark. Could he really already rely so little on his own understanding? If it was possible that he should invite a questionable person into the bank by an explicit letter in order to ask him for advice about his trial, separated from the Deputy Director by only a door, was it not then possible, and even very likely, that he was overlooking other dangers too, or running headlong into them? There was not always someone standing beside him to warn him. And precisely now, when he meant to come forward with all his strength gathered, such doubts about his own vigilance, hitherto foreign to him, had to arise! Were the difficulties that he felt in carrying out his office work now to begin in the trial as well? Now, at any rate, he could no longer comprehend at all how it had been possible that he had wanted to write to Titorelli and invite him into the bank.

He was still shaking his head over it when the attendant came to his side and drew his attention to three gentlemen who were sitting on a bench here in the anteroom. They had already been waiting a long time to be admitted to K. Now that the attendant was speaking with K., they had stood up, and each wanted to make use of a favourable opportunity to get at K. ahead of the others. Since the bank had been so inconsiderate as to let them lose their time here in the waiting room, they too no longer wished to show any consideration. "Chief Clerk," one of them was already saying. But K. had had the attendant bring him his winter coat and, while putting it on with the attendant's help, said to all three: "Forgive me, gentlemen, unfortunately I have no time to receive you at the moment. I do beg your pardon, but I have an urgent business errand to see to and must leave at once. You have seen for yourselves how long I have been held up just now. Would you be so kind as to come back tomorrow or whenever you like? Or shall we perhaps discuss the matters by telephone? Or would you perhaps like to tell me briefly now what it concerns, and I shall then give you a detailed answer in writing. The best thing, though, would be for you to come again soon." These proposals of K.'s threw the gentlemen, who were now to have waited entirely in vain, into such astonishment that they looked at one another without a word. "So we are agreed?" asked K., who had turned round to the attendant, who was now bringing him his hat as well. Through the open door to K.'s room one could see that outside the snowfall had grown much heavier. K. therefore turned up his coat collar and buttoned it high under his chin.
